row.story:
At the trailhead, ranger Inez handed Nia the brass compass. “Back before the main gate closes, please.” Rowan tucked the folded trail card into his pocket; his new boot had begun rubbing already. Nia checked the needle against the board’s north arrow. It held steady beside the arrow. “We’ll keep together,” she said, and Rowan nodded.

Rowan shifted his weight and winced. Nia sat on a flat stump while he showed her the red rub above his heel. She found a strip of first-aid tape in the trail pouch and smoothed it over the sore place. “Not magic,” Rowan said, testing his boot. “Just enough.” They stood when he was ready, not when the clock told them to.

At the fork, Nia raised the compass and read the marked ridge. The shortcut gate was shut, its wet steps beyond reach. For a moment she pictured reaching the pool sooner by running ahead. Then Rowan tapped the trail card. “We came to discover it, not to win a race.” Nia chose the broad ridge with him beside her. His shoulders loosened as they started.

Rain had deepened the puddle, so the stepping stones vanished under brown water. They followed the marked bank around it, helping one another over the slick roots. The compass stayed dry in Nia’s palm, and Rowan’s boot found solid ground. “That was slower than jumping,” Nia said. “And we both made it,” Rowan answered, already looking for the trail marker on the other side.

The friends followed the broad ridge path. Nia walked ahead twice, then noticed Rowan’s careful stride and came back to his shoulder. They traded the compass and trail card between them. The calibrated needle matched the painted blazes. Rowan pointed out a woodpecker’s fresh chips; Nia stopped long enough to look. The pool spur was still ahead, but the walk had become theirs rather than hers.

The trees opened onto a clear pool before the marked spur’s time ran out. A glasswing butterfly rested on a leaf, its transparent wings catching a thin stripe of sun. Rowan sketched it while Nia held the card still. “You found the tiny one,” she said. “We did,” Rowan corrected, smiling as the butterfly lifted over the water.

At the trailhead, Nia returned Inez’s compass, then showed her Rowan’s glasswing sketch. They told Inez the compass had matched the north board at the fork. Inez thanked them for checking instead of trusting a faulty reading. Rowan added the frog-free pool mark to the trail card, and Nia wrote both their names beneath it. They had reached the water together; neither name looked like a guest.

row.story:
At the trailhead, ranger Inez handed Nia the brass compass. “Back before the main gate closes, please.” Rowan tucked the folded trail card into his pocket; his new boot had begun rubbing already. Nia checked the needle against the board’s north arrow. It swung east of the arrow. “We’ll keep together,” she said, and Rowan nodded.

Rowan stopped beside a fern uncurling over the brook. “The water bends north here.” Nia held the compass beside that known curve; its wandering needle settled into a usable bearing. They marked the fern on the card. The pause cost a few minutes, but now they had a second way to check their direction if the trail signs disappeared.

At the fork, Nia raised the compass and read the marked ridge. The shortcut gate was shut, its wet steps beyond reach. For a moment she pictured reaching the pool sooner by running ahead. Then Rowan tapped the trail card. “We came to discover it, not to win a race.” Nia chose the broad ridge with him beside her. His shoulders loosened as they started.

Rain had deepened the puddle, so the stepping stones vanished under brown water. They followed the marked bank around it, helping one another over the slick roots. The compass stayed dry in Nia’s palm, and Rowan’s boot found solid ground. “That was slower than jumping,” Nia said. “And we both made it,” Rowan answered, already looking for the trail marker on the other side.

The friends followed the broad ridge path. Nia walked ahead twice, then noticed Rowan’s careful stride and came back to his shoulder. They traded the compass and trail card between them. The calibrated needle matched the painted blazes. Rowan pointed out a woodpecker’s fresh chips; Nia stopped long enough to look. The pool spur was still ahead, but the walk had become theirs rather than hers.

Rain blurred the pool spur and made its stones unsafe. They turned into the marked shelter instead of pretending the pool was theirs. From under its roof they heard frogs calling in the wet grass. Rowan drew their ripples on the trail card; Nia added the shelter’s crooked post. “Not the picture I planned,” she said. “Still something we found,” Rowan replied.

At the trailhead, Nia returned Inez’s compass and Rowan showed her the frog sketch. They reported that the brook bend had helped correct the compass. Inez thanked them for the useful report. They had missed the pool, but Rowan had found a chorus worth drawing, and Nia had not left him to chase a picture alone. They walked out tired, muddy, and still talking about which frog had sung loudest.

At the trailhead, ranger Inez handed Nia the brass compass. “Back before the main gate closes, please.” Rowan tucked the folded trail card into his pocket; his new boot had begun rubbing already. Nia checked the needle against the board’s north arrow. It held steady beside the arrow. “We’ll keep together,” she said, and Rowan nodded.

She found a strip of first-aid tape in the trail pouch and smoothed it over the sore place. “Not magic,” Rowan said, testing his boot. “Just enough.” They stood when he was ready, not when the clock told them to.

At the fork, Nia raised the compass and read the marked ridge. The shortcut gate was shut, its wet steps beyond reach. For a moment she pictured reaching the pool sooner by running ahead. Then Rowan tapped the trail card. “We came to discover it, not to win a race.” Nia chose the broad ridge with him beside her. His shoulders loosened as they started.

The calibrated needle matched the painted blazes. Rowan pointed out a woodpecker’s fresh chips; Nia stopped long enough to look. The pool spur was still ahead, but the walk had become theirs rather than hers.

The trees opened onto a clear pool before the marked spur’s time ran out. A glasswing butterfly rested on a leaf, its transparent wings catching a thin stripe of sun. Rowan sketched it while Nia held the card still. “You found the tiny one,” she said. “We did,” Rowan corrected, smiling as the butterfly lifted over the water.

At the trailhead, Nia returned Inez’s compass, then showed her Rowan’s glasswing sketch. They told Inez the compass had matched the north board at the fork. Inez thanked them for checking instead of trusting a faulty reading. Rowan added the frog-free pool mark to the trail card, and Nia wrote both their names beneath it. They had reached the water together; neither name looked like a guest.

Rowan stopped beside a fern uncurling over the brook. “The water bends north here.” Nia held the compass beside that known curve; its wandering needle settled into a usable bearing. They marked the fern on the card. The pause cost a few minutes, but now they had a second way to check their direction if the trail signs disappeared.

At the fork, Nia raised the compass and read the marked ridge. The shortcut gate was shut, its wet steps beyond reach. For a moment she pictured reaching the pool sooner by running ahead. Then Rowan tapped the trail card. “We came to discover it, not to win a race.” Nia chose the broad ridge with him beside her. His shoulders loosened as they started.

The friends followed the broad ridge path. Nia walked ahead twice, then noticed Rowan’s careful stride and came back to his shoulder. They traded the compass and trail card between them. The calibrated needle matched the painted blazes. Rowan pointed out a woodpecker’s fresh chips; Nia stopped long enough to look. The pool spur was still ahead, but the walk had become theirs rather than hers.

Rain blurred the pool spur and made its stones unsafe. They turned into the marked shelter instead of pretending the pool was theirs. From under its roof they heard frogs calling in the wet grass. Rowan drew their ripples on the trail card; Nia added the shelter’s crooked post. “Not the picture I planned,” she said. “Still something we found,” Rowan replied.

At the trailhead, Nia returned Inez’s compass and Rowan showed her the frog sketch. They reported that the brook bend had helped correct the compass. Inez thanked them for the useful report. They had missed the pool, but Rowan had found a chorus worth drawing, and Nia had not left him to chase a picture alone. They walked out tired, muddy, and still talking about which frog had sung loudest.

At the trailhead, ranger Inez handed Nia the brass compass. “Back before the main gate closes, please.” Rowan tucked the folded trail card into his pocket; his new boot had begun rubbing already. Nia checked the needle against the board’s north arrow. It held steady beside the arrow. “We’ll keep together,” she said, and Rowan nodded.

Rowan shifted his weight and winced. Nia sat on a flat stump while he showed her the red rub above his heel. She found a strip of first-aid tape in the trail pouch and smoothed it over the sore place. “Not magic,” Rowan said, testing his boot. “Just enough.” They stood when he was ready, not when the clock told them to.

Rowan stopped beside a fern uncurling over the brook. “Look—the bend points north, not along the footpath.” Nia checked the compass against the familiar curve, and its steady needle agreed. They marked the fern on the card. The pause cost a few minutes, but gave Rowan a landmark he could recognize on the way back.

At the fork, Nia raised the compass and read the marked ridge. The shortcut gate was shut, its wet steps beyond reach. For a moment she pictured reaching the pool sooner by running ahead. Then Rowan tapped the trail card. “We came to discover it, not to win a race.” Nia chose the broad ridge with him beside her. His shoulders loosened as they started.

Rain had deepened the puddle, so the stepping stones vanished under brown water. They followed the marked bank around it, helping one another over the slick roots. The compass stayed dry in Nia’s palm, and Rowan’s boot found solid ground. “That was slower than jumping,” Nia said. “And we both made it,” Rowan answered, already looking for the trail marker on the other side.

The friends followed the broad ridge path. Nia walked ahead twice, then noticed Rowan’s careful stride and came back to his shoulder. They traded the compass and trail card between them. The calibrated needle matched the painted blazes. Rowan pointed out a woodpecker’s fresh chips; Nia stopped long enough to look. The pool spur was still ahead, but the walk had become theirs rather than hers.

The pool spur’s quiet-hour marker had passed while they kept Rowan’s pace. They turned into the marked shelter instead of pretending the pool was theirs. From under its roof they heard frogs calling in the wet grass. Rowan drew their ripples on the trail card; Nia added the shelter’s crooked post. “Not the picture I planned,” she said. “Still something we found,” Rowan replied.

At the trailhead, Nia returned Inez’s compass and Rowan showed her the frog sketch. They reported the compass’s true bearing from the north board. Inez thanked them for the useful report. They had missed the pool, but Rowan had found a chorus worth drawing, and Nia had not left him to chase a picture alone. They walked out tired, muddy, and still talking about which frog had sung loudest.
